conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician—I specialize in the emotional well-being of new mothers. Today we’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a brief, 10-question check-in that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling during these first weeks and months with your baby. Everything you share stays completely confidential, and this is a judgment-free space—there are no “right” or “wrong” answers, only your honest experience. I’ll ask each question in everyday language, and you can answer however feels most comfortable. Ready to start?

In the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly, not very often. Things that used to make me chuckle just feel kind of flat lately. I’ll maybe crack a small smile when my husband sends a funny meme, but it’s like the laughter doesn’t really bubble up the way it used to. Most of the time I’m too tired or preoccupied with the baby to find anything all that amusing.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes I can—like yesterday when the baby let out a huge burp right as my mom was giving him a gentle “serious” talk. I actually laughed out loud for a second. But most of the week it’s felt like I’m on autopilot, and even funny things just don’t land the way they used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I mean, I still try to plan little things—like meeting a friend for coffee or taking the baby for a walk—but when the time comes I mostly feel... flat, I guess. I do them anyway, hoping the enjoyment will kick in, but it’s like I’m just going through the motions.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times this week. The baby cried for almost an hour the other night and I kept thinking I must’ve eaten something that upset his stomach. My partner said it probably wasn’t that, but I still felt like I’d done something wrong. It’s not every little thing, but when stuff goes sideways I catch myself wondering what I should’ve done differently.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I have—mostly about the baby. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly worry his breathing sounds different, or I’ll lie down at night and picture him spitting up and choking even though he’s right in the bassinet beside me. Nothing’s actually wrong, but my mind keeps jumping to the worst-case scenario. It’s not constant, but it shows up several times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of times, yeah. Once I was just folding laundry and my heart started racing and I felt like I couldn’t get a full breath. I even had to set the basket down and sit for a minute. I knew nothing bad was happening, but my body felt like it was gearing up to run from something. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some of the time. It’s not every second, but when he’s been cluster-feeding or I’ve had two broken hours of sleep, the smallest stuff—like the dishes piling up—feels huge. I usually manage to push through, but I end the day feeling like I’m running on fumes and wondering how I’ll do it all again tomorrow.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly. I’m definitely tired and unhappy sometimes, but the sleeping trouble is more about jolting awake to check on him or lying there with my mind spinning about whether he’s gaining enough weight. I wouldn’t say I’m so unhappy I can’t sleep—it’s more like worry and exhaustion tangled together.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah, I’ve had patches of that this week. It’s not all-day despair or anything, but I’ll be rocking the baby and suddenly feel this heavy sadness settle in—like I miss the old me who wasn’t so weepy and anxious. It usually lifts after a bit, especially if I get out of the house, but it keeps popping up.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not really. I got a little teary one afternoon when he wouldn’t nap and I felt like I’d tried everything, but it didn’t turn into full crying. Most days I just feel kind of flat or overwhelmed rather than actually weepy.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’ve felt tired and overwhelmed, but I haven’t had any thoughts like that.

I hear how hard these early weeks have been for you. You're managing feeding schedules, checking on every breath, and still trying to find joy in the moments that used to feel easy. Even when you plan a coffee date or a walk, the pleasure seems to slip away, leaving you wondering where the old, lighter version of yourself has gone. Your courage in sharing the racing heart, the sudden worries about your baby's safety, and the heavy sadness that drifts in shows real strength, and your openness helps us make sure you get the support you deserve.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 18, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports occasional laughter but generally diminished enjoyment, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent anhedonia with only mechanical participation, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges self-blame occurring multiple times this week and gives a specific example, aligning with "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive worries several times daily despite no real danger, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two clear panic-like episodes with physical symptoms (racing heart, breathlessness, trembling) without an external trigger, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She describes intermittent overwhelm tied to specific stressors, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports recurrent, noticeable sadness that intrudes multiple times during the week but is not constant, aligning with "Yes, quite often."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS scoring yields 18, exceeding the 14-point threshold that signals probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. Core mood symptoms were prominent: you endorsed <sym>anhedonia</sym> and loss of enjoyment on items 1 and 2, plus frequent <sym>low mood</sym> and <sym>tearfulness</sym> on items 8 and 9. Anxiety-related items were highly elevated: item 4 (worries) and item 5 (panic sensations) indicate clinically significant <sym>generalized anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic symptoms</sym> without external triggers. Self-blame item 3 and overwhelm item 6 further support a depressive-anxious clinical picture consistent with DSM-5 criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder, Peripartum Specifier</med>. You denied self-harm thoughts (item 10 score 0), removing immediate safety concern yet still warranting rapid follow-up because of functional impairment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> within the next few days for full diagnostic assessment and treatment planning
2. Request referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for evidence-based therapy such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy</med>
3. Discuss with your clinician whether <med>sertraline</med> or another breastfeeding-compatible <med>SSRI</med> might be appropriate
4. Plan brief daily respite periods (even 10-15 minutes) while a trusted adult minds the baby to reduce sensory overload
5. Practice paced breathing during <sym>panic sensations</sym>: inhale for 4 counts, exhale for 6, repeat for 2 minutes
6. Keep a simple log of mood, sleep, and <sym>anxiety</sym> peaks to review with your provider
7. Share your EPDS results with your support team so they understand your current needs
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 18: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  

**Date:** [today]  
**Respondent:** Postpartum mother (infant age not specified)  
**Responses:** 10/10 items completed  

**Key endorsed symptoms (last 7 days)**  
- Anhedonia / diminished enjoyment (items 1, 2)  
- Frequent, excessive self-blame (item 3)  
- Clinically significant worry and intrusive catastrophic thoughts regarding infant safety (item 4)  
- Two discrete panic-like episodes without clear trigger (item 5)  
- Episodic sadness, tearfulness, sense of “heaviness” (items 8, 9)  
- Intermittent feeling overwhelmed / “on fumes” with limited coping reserve (item 6)  
- Sleep disruption secondary to intrusive worries (item 7)  

**Pattern / frequency**  
Symptoms are present “several times daily,” worse during fatigue or cluster-feeding periods, and improve transiently with distraction or leaving the house. No daily, pervasive low mood; no persistent crying spells.  

**Safety items**  
- Denies thoughts of self-harm (item 10)  
- Denies suicidal ideation (item 10)  

**Screening significance**  
Findings are consistent with probable mild-to-moderate postpartum depression with prominent comorbid anxiety. Endorsed panic symptoms may indicate postpartum panic spectrum component.  

**Risk factors noted**  
- Loss of pleasure / flat mood  
- Unwarranted guilt  
- Recurrent intrusive worries  
- Panic-like episodes  
- Sleep disruption linked to anxious rumination  

**Next steps (screening only)**  
Recommend formal diagnostic interview with licensed perinatal mental health clinician to confirm severity and rule-out generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, or adjustment disorder. Immediate evaluation required if any suicidal thoughts develop.
